summary: Describes a set of assembly-language subprograms at the University of California, Santa Barbara that let Fortran programs on its IBM 360/75 use the network. The routines sit between the programmer and the local Network Control Program. Each open socket has a completion code variable that tracks its status.

plainLanguage.summary: A cook who only speaks one language uses a translator to order from a faraway kitchen. These Fortran routines are the translator between programs and the network.

subtitle: Assembly-language routines that let Fortran programs on UCSB's 360/75 open, use and close ARPANET sockets.

tldr.problem: Fortran programmers at UCSB had no direct way to use the network through the local Network Control Program (NCP).
tldr.mechanism: A set of assembly-language subprograms (OPEN, CLOSE, SEND, RECEIVE, CHECK, ID, SIGNAL and Online System routines) wraps NCP operations, using a per-socket completion code variable that reports each result.
tldr.outcome: They were implemented at UCSB and are callable from any Fortran main program or subroutine compiled there.

today: RFC 119 documents a 1971 site-specific interface at UCSB, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text does not describe any use beyond UCSB.

sections.title: What the Subprograms Are
sections.content:
M. Krilanovich of UCSB describes subroutines that make the Network accessible, via the NCP, to Fortran programs running on the 360/75. They are written in assembly language and act as an interface between the user and the Network Control Program, which supervises all Network operations at the site.

They can be called from any Fortran main program or subroutine compiled at UCSB.
sections.plainLanguage: Fortran programs could not talk to the network by themselves, so a set of ready-made helper routines does it for them.

sections.title: Completion Codes, Time Limits and Sockets
sections.content:
Each socket that is not closed has a unique completion code variable. It identifies the local socket, and when an operation finishes it holds a code for the outcome. It must be of type INTEGER*4. Its starting value does not matter, and the programmer may use it for other purposes.

Most subprograms start the operation and wait, using no CPU time, until the NCP reports completion. The programmer gives a time limit in tenths of a second. If it is exceeded, code 252 is returned, control goes back to the caller and the operation is still pending. A code of 0 means success.

A socket is named by an INTEGER*4 array: the first element is the site number and the next is the socket number. A socket number may be positive, negative or zero, and it is even or odd by its absolute value, which sets its gender.
sections.plainLanguage: Each open phone line gets its own sticky note. The helper writes on it how the call went, and it will only wait a limited time for a pick-up before telling you it ran out of time.

sections.title: The Subprograms
sections.content:
OPEN takes a closed local socket out of that state in three ways. CONNECT links it to a foreign socket and waits for acceptance or rejection. LISTEN waits for a call to the local socket. ACCEPT completes a connection after a successful LISTEN. CLOSE returns a socket to the closed state; it refuses a pending call, aborts a connection attempt, or lets data in transit arrive first.

SEND is invoked as CALL WRITE (cmpcd, bfr, len, time [,offset]) and RECEIVE as CALL READ with the same shape. The length is in bits and the optional offset is a bit offset into the buffer. CHECK returns a status code and mnemonic (such as OPEN, LISTEN, CONNECT, I/O, CLOSED or CLOSING), the foreign socket and a send or receive deficit in bits, and it always completes immediately. ID returns the socket identifier for a completion code variable, or zero. SIGNAL sends a user-defined signal that makes the foreign socket's next SEND or RECEIVE be suppressed with a code saying a signal arrived.

Each operation lists its own completion codes, for example 20 when a connection attempt is rejected by the foreign process and 44 when an operator command terminated all Network operations.
sections.plainLanguage: There are routines to dial, to answer, to hang up, to talk, to listen, to check the line, and to tap the other side on the shoulder.

sections.title: Online System Message Conventions
sections.content:
Some subprograms are meant for the Online System Network operators. Their data is grouped in messages of three fields: an op code (one byte), a length (two bytes, giving the length in bits of the text) and the text. The op code and length together are the header.

Op code 0 is a NOP used mainly as a delimiter, and 1 means EBCDIC characters for display. Codes 2 and 3 carry keypushes, to be executed at once or after all data for that receive has arrived. A standard string of messages ends with a NOP header called a trailer. WTOLC, write to online console, sends EBCDIC characters in a standard message with a header and optionally a trailer. These conventions are the default and can be overridden by programming.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note has a small label saying what kind of thing is inside and how long it is, and a blank note at the end means, that is all.

items.label: NOP
items.desc: No text field; used mainly as a delimiter.

items.label: EBCDIC text
items.desc: One character per byte, for display once received.

items.label: Keypushes
items.desc: One byte per key, executed once the text is received.

items.label: Delayed keypushes
items.desc: Execution waits until all data for that receive has arrived.
